claim: Compare two ways to hold a sum for ten years: buy a 10-year Treasury note at that month's yield and hold it, or keep rolling 3-month Treasury bills. Over 762 starting months from April 1953 to September 2016, rolling bills ended with more money in 32.68% of cases. The pattern is concentrated: bills won in 85.42% of starting months from 1960 to 1979, when inflation and rates were building, but in only 2.27% of starting months since 1980, when rates were mostly falling. The best case for bills left them 24.8% ahead after ten years; the best case for the note left it 103.4% ahead. Which choice won depended on the path of rates after purchase, not on the note's higher starting yield.

numbers.definition: Starting months s in the GS10 file (monthly average 10-year constant-maturity Treasury yield, percent) for which TB3MS (3-month Treasury bill secondary market rate, percent, monthly) exists for all 120 months s..s+119.

Share of starting months with Bills/Note > 1, x100, where Bills = product over k=0..119 of (1 + TB3MS(s+k)/1200) and Note = (1 + GS10(s)/200)^20 (par note, semiannual coupons reinvested at the purchase yield).
Same share restricted to starting months 1960-01..1979-12.
Same share restricted to starting months 1980-01 onward.
(max over starting months of Bills/Note - 1) x 100.
(1 / min over starting months of Bills/Note - 1) x 100.

assumptions: Bills: each month earns TB3MS/12 (the quoted discount-basis annual rate, used as a simple monthly return), compounded monthly for 120 months, no taxes or fees.
Note: bought at par at the purchase month's average constant-maturity yield; coupons reinvested at that yield, so ending value = (1 + y/2)^20.
Both strategies are nominal and before tax; inflation affects both equally.
